title: Arranging Coins
description: Brute force to optimized: row-by-row simulation versus binary search using the closed-form triangular number formula.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: You have n coins and want to build a staircase where row 1 has 1 coin, row 2 has 2 coins, and so on, row k has k coins. Given n, return the number of COMPLETE rows that can be formed (a row is only counted if it is entirely filled).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n, the total number of coins"],["Output","The number of complete staircase rows formable"],["Goal","Find the answer in O(log n), exploiting the monotonic growth of triangular numbers"],["Constraints","1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"How many complete rows/steps fit within a budget,\" with each step costing more than the last","Binary search on the answer, since the cumulative cost (a triangular number) grows monotonically"],["A closed-form formula exists for the cumulative cost of k rows","Directly compare the formula's value to n at each binary search step, no simulation needed"]]}

blocks.text: The total coins needed to complete k rows is 1+2+...+k, the k-th triangular number, k*(k+1)/2. As k increases, this total strictly increases, so finding the largest k whose triangular number does not exceed n is a monotonic search problem.

blocks.title: Analogy: Stacking Bricks in Increasingly Wide Rows
blocks.text: Picture stacking bricks into a triangle shape, where each new row needs one more brick than the last. Given a fixed brick supply, you want to know how many COMPLETE rows you can build before running out, without wasting bricks on a half-finished row.

blocks.caption: The cumulative coins needed through row k is a triangular number, growing monotonically with k

blocks.text: Result: 2. Row 1 needs 1 coin (total 1), row 2 needs 2 more (total 3), row 3 would need 3 more (total 6, exceeding 5), so only 2 complete rows fit, with 2 coins left over.

Before simulating row by row, notice that the total coins used through row k has a closed-form formula (a triangular number) that grows monotonically with k, which is exactly the structure binary search exploits to find the largest valid k directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The total coins used through row k is exactly k*(k+1)/2, the well-known triangular number formula.

Observation 2: This value strictly increases as k increases, so there is a clean threshold: the largest k for which k*(k+1)/2 <= n is the answer.

Observation 3: Binary searching over candidate k values in [0, n], comparing k*(k+1)/2 to n at each step, converges on this threshold in O(log n) instead of simulating each row one at a time.

Observation 4: Care is needed with integer overflow for large n and k in fixed-width-integer languages, since k*(k+1) can be large before dividing by 2.
This leads to binary searching over candidate row counts k in [0, n], comparing the triangular number formula k*(k+1)/2 directly to n, narrowing the range until the largest valid k is found.
Simulate building rows one at a time: subtract the required coins for each next row from a running total, stopping when there are not enough coins left for the next row.

items: Start with row = 1 and remaining = n.
While remaining coins are at least equal to the current row number, subtract that many coins and move to the next row.
Return one less than the final row number (the count of fully completed rows).

codes.python:
def arrange_coins_brute(n):
    row = 1
    remaining = n
    while remaining >= row:                  # simulate one row at a time
        remaining -= row
        row += 1
    return row - 1

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Simulating each row directly follows the problem's physical description, easy to reason about.
For large n (up to about 2^31 - 1), the number of rows can be around 65000, requiring that many iterations, more than necessary given the closed-form formula.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(sqrt(n)), since the number of complete rows is roughly proportional to sqrt(n).
Space: O(1).

Limitation: although O(sqrt(n)) is already reasonably fast, binary search using the closed-form triangular number formula achieves O(log n), a further improvement, and demonstrates the more broadly reusable "binary search on the answer" technique.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why simulating row by row is unnecessary: the total coins used through row k has an exact closed-form formula, k*(k+1)/2, so there is no need to accumulate a running total step by step.

The binary search approach: since this formula strictly increases with k, binary search over candidate k values directly finds the largest k satisfying k*(k+1)/2 <= n.

Handling the comparison: at each candidate k, compute k*(k+1)/2 (using a wide enough integer type to avoid overflow) and compare it to n, narrowing the search range accordingly.

The core idea: binary search on the answer, using the triangular number formula as a direct O(1) computation instead of an O(sqrt(n)) simulation.
Binary search over k in [0, n]. At each step, compute k*(k+1)/2 and compare to n; if equal, return k; if less, search higher; if greater, search lower. Return the largest k found not exceeding n.

blocks.caption: Binary search directly on k, comparing the triangular number formula to n

blocks.text: Since k*(k+1)/2 strictly increases as k increases, binary search correctly narrows toward the exact threshold: any k with total <= n is a feasible candidate (search continues higher to find a possibly larger valid k), and any k with total > n is infeasible (search moves lower). When the search range is exhausted, hi holds the largest feasible k, exactly the number of complete rows.

blocks.text: Arranging Coins is a clean example of "binary search on the answer" combined with a closed-form formula, replacing an O(sqrt(n)) simulation with an O(log n) direct search.

items: Integer overflow when computing k*(k+1) for large n in fixed-width-integer languages, mitigated by using a wide integer type.
Returning lo instead of hi (or vice versa) at the end, an off-by-one that misses the correct final answer.

blocks.text: Recognizing the triangular number formula and framing this explicitly as "binary search on the answer using a monotonic closed-form formula" demonstrates strong pattern transfer from more literal binary-search problems.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how many complete steps fit within a growing-cost budget", think: binary search on the step count, using a closed-form cumulative-cost formula if one exists.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The row-by-row simulation runs in O(sqrt(n)) time; binary search with the triangular number formula runs in O(log n) time, both using O(1) space.

Core Idea: binary search candidate row counts k, comparing k*(k+1)/2 to n directly instead of simulating row by row.
Time: O(sqrt(n)) for the simulation, O(log n) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: recognizing the triangular number formula turns a simulation into a direct, monotonic binary search target.
